description: Tenses indicate the time and state of an action. Conditional Sentences express the circumstances under which an action takes place or could take place. In competitive exams, error-spotting questions based on these concepts are frequently asked.

sections.title: Simple Tenses
sections.description: Simple Tenses are used to indicate habits, facts, and events occurring at a specific time.

key_concepts.explanation: It is used to express universal truths, habits, and daily routines.
It indicates actions that were completed at a specific time in the past. It is often used with time expressions like yesterday, ago, or last year.

grammar_rules.structure: Subject + V1 (s/es with 3rd person singular) + Object
grammar_rules.explanation: We add 's' or 'es' to the base form of the verb when the subject is singular (third person).
The second form of the verb (V2) is used in affirmative sentences.

examples.incorrect_or_context: He have passed the exam last year.
examples.correct_or_usage: He passed the exam last year.
examples.explanation: The phrase 'last year' indicates a specific past time, so the Simple Past (V2) must be used here instead of the Present Perfect.

sections.title: Perfect Tenses
sections.description: Perfect Tenses indicate actions that have already been completed before a specific point in time.

key_concepts.explanation: It indicates actions that have recently been completed or whose effect is still felt in the present.
When two actions occurred in the past, the action that finished first is written in the Past Perfect, and the one that happened later is written in the Simple Past.

grammar_rules.explanation: If no specific past time is given and the action has relevance to the present, use the Present Perfect tense.

grammar_rules.structure: 1st Action: Sub + had + V3 | 2nd Action: Sub + V2
grammar_rules.explanation: This structure is used to show a chronological sequence between two past events.

examples.incorrect_or_context: The patient died before the doctor came.
examples.correct_or_usage: The patient had died before the doctor came.
examples.explanation: The patient dying is the first action in the sequence, so it must be expressed in the Past Perfect tense (had died).

sections.title: Real Conditionals (Zero & First)
sections.description: These are sentences where there is a high probability of the condition being fulfilled, or they represent universal truths.

grammar_rules.explanation: Used to state scientific facts, general truths, and habits that are always true.

grammar_rules.structure: If + Simple Present, Simple Future (will/shall + V1)
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to indicate potential future events where the condition is in the present and the result will happen in the future.

examples.incorrect_or_context: If you will work hard, you will pass.
examples.correct_or_usage: If you work hard, you will pass.
examples.explanation: The future tense (will/shall) is never used in the 'If-clause'. It must be kept in the Simple Present tense.

strategies.title: Identify the Condition Clause
strategies.detail: Look for conditional words like 'if', 'unless', 'until', or 'when' in the sentence. Using modal verbs like 'will', 'shall', or 'would' in the clause immediately following these words is a grammatical error.

sections.title: Unreal Conditionals (Second & Third)
sections.description: These are sentences that are hypothetical, imaginary, or represent past conditions that were never fulfilled.

grammar_rules.structure: If + Simple Past (V2), Subject + would + V1
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to indicate an unreal, imaginary, or highly unlikely situation in the present or future.

grammar_rules.structure: If + Past Perfect (had + V3), Subject + would have + V3
grammar_rules.explanation: Used to express a past condition that was not fulfilled and its hypothetical past result.

examples.incorrect_or_context: If I was a bird, I would fly in the sky.
examples.correct_or_usage: If I were a bird, I would fly in the sky.
examples.explanation: In hypothetical or imaginary conditional sentences, 'were' is used with all subjects, regardless of whether they are singular or plural.

examples.incorrect_or_context: If he worked hard, he would have passed.
examples.correct_or_usage: If he had worked hard, he would have passed.
examples.explanation: Since the main clause uses 'would have + V3', the 'If-clause' must follow the Third Conditional structure and use the Past Perfect (had + V3).

sections.title: Exceptions and Special Rules
sections.description: There are some special structures in tenses and conditional sentences that bypass the standard grammatical rules.

grammar_rules.structure: Had + Subject + V3, Subject + would have + V3
grammar_rules.explanation: In Third Conditional sentences, the word 'If' can be omitted, and the sentence can start directly with 'Had' by applying the rule of inversion.

examples.incorrect_or_context: Had I known about the exam, I would prepare better.
examples.correct_or_usage: Had I known about the exam, I would have prepared better.
examples.explanation: The inverted structure 'Had + V3' acts as a past perfect condition, so it must always be followed by 'would have + V3' in the main clause.

exceptions.explanation: Sometimes the result of a past unfulfilled condition is felt in the present. In such cases, the If-clause of the Third Conditional is combined with the main clause of the Second Conditional.
exceptions.example: If I had studied harder (past condition), I would be an engineer now (present result).
